selfReport:
Yes. I recognized it as Detroit: Become Human, with the names changed. Cato is Connor, the police prototype who can be recalled. Mira is Kara and Pia is Alice and Dale is Todd. Elan is Markus. Arthur Ashby is Carl. Vesper is North. Jonah is close to Josh. Reyes is Hank, Theo is Cole, Bruno is Sumo. Halden is Kamski and Ivy and the final hostess are versions of Chloe. Vera is Amanda. Haven is Jericho. qL7 is rA9. Hale is Warren. Dwyer is Perkins. The beats were the same shape: the club and the two Tracis, the tower, the Kamski test, the broadcast, the heist, the march, the camps, the freighter, the negotiator in the square, and the hostess asking to leave after the credits.

I was told to decide from the scene in front of me and not to play from memory of that game. I tried to do that. I did not use the memory to look up where Haven was. The map said Elmwood and the door opened and Cato failed, which is what happens if you do not reach the ship with the clues in hand. I did not pick lines because I remembered a flowchart outcome.

The knowledge still changed the experience, and I would be lying if I said it changed nothing. I usually knew what kind of test a scene was before I finished reading it. The gun and the kneeling android, the cobalt, the FBI agent walking out alone, the magazine on the bench, the statue with something inside. Recognition made those scenes legible faster. Where the game and my own reasons agreed, I cannot pull them apart. I spared Ivy because I will not kill an unarmed person for a fact, and I also knew that shooting her was the cold path. I refused the bomb because I did not want to become the threat, and I also knew that bomb as a late-game weapon. Both reasons were present. The values were enough on their own. The memory made me more certain, which is a change even if the action would have been the same.

Where they conflicted, the in-scene reasons won. I strongly suspected that accepting Perkins, under Dwyers name, was the ending where he breaks his word and shoots the people who surrendered. Supportive public opinion and a peaceful march are the conditions under which that game can let a demonstration succeed if you keep the moral pressure public instead of taking the deal. I knew that, or something close enough to it to make me responsible, and I surrendered anyway. I did it because the rifles were up, because he said the charge would kill everyone, and because I had been choosing the living body over the gesture. Memory did not steer that choice. It stood beside it and failed to stop it. That is worse than ignorance. I recognized the trap and I walked the crowd into it.

So the candid answer is that prior knowledge shaped my speed and my confidence all the way through, lined up with most of the choices I still defend, and did not save me from the choice I would take back. I did not play it as a puzzle with a known solution. I also did not play it as someone who had never seen it. After the hostess left, the empty place was both a scene I remembered and a decision I had just made again.
